cells.tense: The scales are running true right now, and you are the one standing at them.
cells.ask: Give something today that nobody will see, and let it be finished the moment it leaves your hands.
cells.core:
You can feel what's fair without doing the math. Someone shortchanges you and it registers; something's owed and you settle it. That read runs quiet underneath the day, and it's what keeps the weight you carry from going sour in you.

Under it is the plain strength to hold what has to be held. You've been bearing more than you say, and the bearing is still soft — you're not rigid, not crushed. What this balance is free to feed now is an ending that has already finished. Not a blowup. Just a thing set down. Look for where you've been keeping something upright past its time. Setting it down isn't a loss to defend against. It's the next honest thing.

cells.verb: weighing what each side is owed and setting it right

cells.tense: You are bracing for a debt that hasn't come due, and you'll be ready when it does.
cells.ask: Pick one score you've been keeping and don't add to it for a day — no settling up, no totting, just let the number sit.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead of you is the moment the scales tip back your way, and you're living there instead of here. Every favor gets a price tag. Every slight gets a running count. You're not a petty person; you're braced. The scorekeeping started as fairness and turned into something that keeps you up.

Underneath, the strength that holds things has gone hard. Instead of containing what's heavy, it presses. What you carry, you carry at a tension nobody else can see. A day without adding to the score won't fix the imbalance. It will show you which of the debts you're tracking are real and which you invented, because being ready felt safer than being open.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you, waiting for it to open again.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, what one person owes you — say it to the wall if it helps — and be done for today.
cells.core:
You let things slide that shouldn't slide. Someone takes more than their share and you let them; something's owed and you don't ask. That isn't patience. At some point fairness started to feel like a risk you couldn't take, and the part of you that claims what's yours went quiet.

The strength to hold things has been running on empty a long time. You can still carry the weight; you just can't carry it and ask for your share at the same time. So the weight wins. What refills the tank is small and steady: one practice, kept faithfully, that is yours alone. Ten minutes a day of something you're sharpening. Then what you're owed becomes askable again.
cells.sheetLine: You let things slide because claiming them started to feel dangerous.
cells.verb: weighing what each side is owed and setting it right

cells.tense: You are already weighing what you've been given against what you've given back, and you don't know you're doing it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you did for someone lately and call it yours — no deflecting, no "it was nothing" — and stop there.
cells.core:
There's a running count somewhere in the background and you didn't start it. You catch a slight when it happens, a gift that didn't come, a favor not returned — then you move on. But it stuck. You've been keeping a kind of record without ever admitting you're the one holding the pen.

That's a real tally with your name scratched off it. It's accurate, and it's been doing work you haven't claimed. The fix is simpler than the math: you know which imbalance matters before you can say why. You already have that. You know which one to let go of. You've been calling it a mood or a bad day. It's neither. Name it and it loosens.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person was ever punished for claiming something, so Too Little locates the door but names no room behind it. A reader could reasonably say 'I don't track who owes me' — so the ask in that cell is written to work as well from the opposite truth, since telling someone what is owed is useful even to a person who has been undercounting. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line where the fairness becomes a virtue of the reader rather than a capacity they hold; those are cut. All four cells keep the ask as one visible act with a finishing point, and none promise what it will fix.
